newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judges refuse to ban "Larry Flynt" posters.
newsitem.headline: French judges refuse to ban "Larry Flynt" posters.

text.p: French judges refused on Thursday to ban posters advertising "The People vs Larry Flynt", a Hollywood film about pornography and press freedom, after complaints that they offended Christians.

Judges Yves Breillat and Francine Levon-Gerin rejected pleas by a group of Roman Catholics and a right-wing association that the posters, showing a semi-nude actor in a crucifix-like pose, were an infringement on religious freedom.
"This advertisement...does not seem to reveal the slightest attack on any religion or religious group," Breillat wrote in a ruling approving the posters on billboards around France.
The posters show actor Woody Harrelson, arms outstretched, wearing only briefs made of the Stars and Stripes flag, against a backdrop of a woman's bikini-clad loins.

Breillat said the poster was "deliberately provocative" but noted that no actual crucifix appeared in the poster and that the actor's expression did not match traditional depictions of a suffering Jesus Christ.
Alexandre Varaut, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said he would appeal against the ruling.
The film, directed by Milos Forman, won two Oscar nominations last week and opened in France on Wednesday amid a blaze of publicity, largely generated by the posters.

A public prosecutor had urged the courts on Tuesday to ban the posters on the ground that they caused an illegal affront. Lawyers for the producers Columbia Pictures, a unit of Sony Corp, argued they were protected by freedom of expression.

The posters sparked separate lawsuits from about 30 Roman Catholics, led by two priests, and an association close to the extreme-right National Front that says it aims to combat racism and promote French identity.

The town of Versailles, west of Paris, asked the company to take down the posters on Wednesday after the mayor said he received a string of complaints. Bishops also criticised the poster in a country where most people are nominally Catholic.
The film depicts the tumultuous life of publisher Larry Flynt, a school drop-out who ran strip clubs in Ohio before launching his successful magazine Hustler in 1973.

The poster was rejected by the Motion Picture Association of America. In Australia, it was branded degrading and offensive to women and Christians by the Womens' Electoral Lobby and the Catholic Church.

In 1984, a French court banned an advertisment for the film "Ave Maria" which used a semi-naked woman in a crucifix-like position, on the grounds that it was an intrusion into individual religious convictions.
